# Predicting breeding values: GBLUP, BayesA, BayesB {#sec-genomic-prediction} Three earlier chapters flagged the same gap and moved on. @sec-simulating-crosses built `ctx$traits` from *known* marker effects and called the result "an optimistic ceiling." @sec-choosing's Finding 5 showed what happens once the index carries real error, but manufactured that error rather than fitting a model to produce it. @sec-case-study repeats the caveat and still moves on. This chapter is where the gap closes: it fits actual prediction models to a training population with real phenotypic noise, and hands the result to the same `stage1_build()` contract every later chapter already consumes. `vanraden_G()` has said since @sec-coancestry that its matrix "is the right matrix for GBLUP." Nothing in the package has used it that way until now. ## A training population with real noise Everywhere else in this book, `ctx$index` *is* the truth. Here it plays a different role: it is the value a real breeding programme does not get to see, and can only estimate from phenotypes recorded on a subset of individuals. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ctx <- simulate_data(book_cfg) N <- ctx$N g <- ctx$traits[, 1] # the true genetic value -- known only to us ``` ::: A phenotype is the genetic value plus environmental noise, $y = g + e$, and heritability is the fraction of phenotypic variance the genetic part accounts for, $h^2 = \mathrm{Var}(g) / (\mathrm{Var}(g) + \mathrm{Var}(e))$. `traits` is built by `scale()`, so $\mathrm{Var}(g) = 1$ exactly, and the noise variance that delivers a target $h^2$ is $(1-h^2)/h^2$: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} h2 <- 0.5 set.seed(9) e <- rnorm(N, 0, sqrt((1 - h2) / h2)) y <- g + e ``` ::: Split the population into a training set, whose phenotypes the model gets to see, and a candidate set -- the hybrids actually being selected among -- whose phenotypes it does not: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(9) train <- sample.int(N, floor(0.6 * N)) cand <- setdiff(seq_len(N), train) c(train = length(train), candidates = length(cand)) #> train candidates #> 375 250 ``` ::: ## GBLUP: prediction from the relationship matrix GBLUP treats the breeding value as a random effect $\mathbf{u}$ with covariance proportional to the genomic relationship matrix, $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{G}\,\sigma_u^2$, and solves the mixed model equations $$\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1} & \mathbf{1}'\mathbf{Z} \\ \mathbf{Z}'\mathbf{1} & \mathbf{Z}'\mathbf{Z} + \mathbf{G}^{-1}\lambda \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\hat\mu \\ \hat{\mathbf{u}}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{y} \\ \mathbf{Z}'\mathbf{y}\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \lambda = \sigma_e^2/\sigma_u^2,$$ with $\mathbf{Z}$ the incidence matrix mapping training records to individuals. $\mathbf{u}$ is defined over *all* $N$ individuals, training and candidates together, so one solve produces predictions for both. $\lambda$ is exactly $(1-h^2)/h^2$ once traits are standardised, the same ratio used to build `e` above. `vanraden_G()`'s $\mathbf{G}$ is blended a small amount with the identity before inverting -- standard practice, and necessary here because `$G` can be ill-conditioned at $N < m$: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} G <- ctx$G gblup <- function(y, train, h2) { Gstar <- 0.95 * G + 0.05 * diag(N) n_t <- length(train) Z <- matrix(0, n_t, N); Z[cbind(seq_len(n_t), train)] <- 1 X1 <- matrix(1, n_t, 1); lambda <- (1 - h2) / h2 LHS <- rbind(cbind(crossprod(X1), crossprod(X1, Z)), cbind(crossprod(Z, X1), crossprod(Z) + solve(Gstar) * lambda)) RHS <- rbind(crossprod(X1, y[train]), crossprod(Z, y[train])) solve(LHS, RHS)[-1] } u_hat <- gblup(y, train, h2) cat("GBLUP accuracy (candidates):", cor(u_hat[cand], g[cand]), "\n") #> GBLUP accuracy (candidates): 0.9596232 ``` ::: ## BayesA and BayesB: prediction from marker effects GBLUP assumes every marker contributes an equal, infinitesimal share of the genetic variance. The Bayesian alphabet [@meuwissen2001; @delcampos2013] relaxes that one assumption at a time. **BayesA** gives every marker its own variance, drawn from a scaled-inverse-$\chi^2$ prior -- effects are shrunk individually rather than uniformly, which matters when a few markers carry much more signal than the rest. **BayesB** adds a point mass at zero: each marker has prior probability $\pi$ of being excluded entirely, so the model performs variable selection as it fits. Both reduce to GBLUP's ridge-regression solution as a special case; they differ only in how much of the genetic architecture they let the data shape. This book fits both with `bWGR::BayesA()`/`bWGR::BayesB()` [@xavier2019bwgr] rather than by hand -- unlike GBLUP, a Gibbs sampler over marker effects is not the few lines the mixed-model solve above was, and `bWGR` is exactly the tool `vanraden_G()`'s docstring pointed toward without naming: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(bWGR) M <- ctx$X * 2 # dosage 0/1/2, what bWGR expects fitA <- BayesA(y[train], M[train, ], it = 1500, bi = 500, df = 5, R2 = 0.5) fitB <- BayesB(y[train], M[train, ], it = 1500, bi = 500, pi = 0.95, df = 5, R2 = 0.5) predA <- as.numeric(M[cand, ] %*% fitA$b) predB <- as.numeric(M[cand, ] %*% fitB$b) c(BayesA = cor(predA, g[cand]), BayesB = cor(predB, g[cand])) #> BayesA BayesB #> 0.9608579 0.9600266 ``` ::: Both fits produce a marker-effect vector `$b`; a candidate's GEBV is just its genotypes dotted with those effects. GBLUP produced the same quantity from the relationship matrix instead of the markers directly -- two routes to the same thing, checked next. ## Verification: two routes agree GBLUP with a flat prior on every marker's variance and the un-selected member of the Bayesian alphabet, Bayesian ridge regression (`iv = FALSE, pi = 0` in `bWGR::wgr()`), are the same model solved two different ways -- one through the $N \times N$ relationship matrix, the other through the $N \times m$ marker matrix. They should agree, and at this book's scale checking that costs one more fit: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} yobs <- rep(NA_real_, N); yobs[train] <- y[train] fit_brr <- wgr(yobs, M, iv = FALSE, pi = 0, it = 1500, bi = 500) c(worst_case_disagreement = cor(u_hat, fit_brr$hat - mean(fit_brr$hat))) #> worst_case_disagreement #> 0.9992545 ``` ::: The correlation between the two routes, computed over all 625 individuals, is 0.999 -- not exact, because the Gibbs sampler is stochastic and the relationship-blend used above has no exact marker-space equivalent, but close enough to confirm neither route has a bug the other would not share. ## Which model wins, and when `ctx$traits` is built from thousands of markers with independent, similarly sized effects -- the textbook case GBLUP's infinitesimal-model assumption was designed for. A trait controlled by a handful of large-effect loci is a different regime, and it is the one BayesB's point-mass prior exists for. `book/scripts/regenerate.R genpred` reruns the fits above 15 times each, at two heritabilities, under both `ctx$traits`'s polygenic architecture and a book-local variant with genetic variance concentrated on three markers out of 2000: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Mean prediction accuracy (correlation, candidates only) over 15 independent training/candidate splits. |arch | h2| GBLUP| BayesA| BayesB| |:----------|---:|-----:|------:|------:| |oligogenic | 0.2| 0.789| 0.782| 0.788| |polygenic | 0.2| 0.799| 0.795| 0.798| |oligogenic | 0.5| 0.930| 0.931| 0.952| |polygenic | 0.5| 0.935| 0.935| 0.934| ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sub <- reshape(acc, direction = "long", varying = c("GBLUP", "BayesA", "BayesB"), v.names = "accuracy", timevar = "method", times = c("GBLUP", "BayesA", "BayesB")) sub$grp <- interaction(sub$arch, sub$h2, sep = "\nh2=") boxplot(accuracy ~ method + grp, sub, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7, col = rep(c("grey85", "grey65", "grey45"), 4), ylab = "accuracy (candidates)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Prediction accuracy by architecture and heritability, 15 replicate splits each.](08b-genomic-prediction_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1050} ::: ::: At $h^2 = 0.5$ under the oligogenic architecture, BayesB's mean accuracy is 0.022 higher than GBLUP's -- the gap the model was built to close. Under the polygenic architecture the three methods are indistinguishable within replicate noise: with genetic variance spread over thousands of markers, BayesB's variable selection has nothing to select, and its point-mass prior buys nothing GBLUP was not already doing. **The `pi = 0.95` above was fixed, not tuned.** A real analyst does not know the true sparsity in advance. `genpred`'s second sweep holds the oligogenic architecture and $h^2 = 0.5$ fixed and only moves `pi`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: BayesB accuracy as `pi` moves from far too lenient toward the true sparsity (3 causal markers of 2000, pi = 0.9985). | pi| BayesB| |-----:|------:| | 0.500| 0.948| | 0.900| 0.955| | 0.950| 0.958| | 0.990| 0.964| | 0.995| 0.967| ::: ::: Accuracy improves monotonically as `pi` approaches the truth, but the degradation from being off is gradual, not catastrophic -- `pi` is worth worth cross-validating, not agonising over -- see the closing note below. ## From GEBVs to `stage1_build()` Everything above ends where @sec-simulating-crosses's contract begins. The candidates' predicted values, whichever model produced them, are exactly the `traits` argument `stage1_build()` expects -- one column per trait, one row per hybrid: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hybrids_traits <- data.frame(hybrid = cand, trait1 = predB) head(hybrids_traits) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| hybrid| trait1| |------:|----------:| | 4| -2.1452967| | 5| -1.9589815| | 6| -2.4404613| | 11| -0.6052611| | 13| -1.0057744| | 16| -2.0736992|
::: ::: Repeat the fit once per trait in the multi-trait index and this data frame is what feeds `stage1_build(X, ped, traits, fL)`. Everything from @sec-ocs onward already assumes exactly this shape; this chapter is only the part that used to be silent about where it comes from. ## Back to Finding 5: a measured accuracy, not an assumed one @sec-choosing's Finding 5 assumed a prediction accuracy `r` and manufactured error correlated with relatedness to match it. The GBLUP fit above at $h^2 = 0.5$ gives a *measured* accuracy of 0.96 on the polygenic architecture -- near the high end of the range Finding 5 explored ($r \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1\}$), a reminder that a well-powered training set at $h^2 = 0.5$ is a comparatively easy case -- and its errors are, in fact, structured by relatedness rather than white: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} err <- g[cand] - u_hat[cand] fcand <- ctx$f[cand, cand] ut <- upper.tri(fcand) cor(outer(err, err)[ut], fcand[ut]) #> [1] 0.1397751 ``` ::: Pairs of candidates that are more related have more correlated prediction errors -- the mechanism Finding 5 assumed, confirmed here from an actual fitted model rather than injected. It is a modest correlation, not the extreme case Finding 5 stress-tested, because $h^2 = 0.5$ with `r length(train)` training records is a comparatively favourable regime; a smaller or less related training set would push it higher. ::: {.callout-note} ## What this chapter still does not model Closing the "traits are given" gap opens several more, named here so they are not silently dropped: - **Hybrid-specific prediction.** The GEBV above is additive, predicted from the hybrid's own dosage. It says nothing about specific combining ability -- @sec-heterosis's dominance deviation $H_i$ is a separate quantity, and a full hybrid-prediction model would estimate GCA and SCA jointly rather than fitting one additive effect per marker. - **Multivariate prediction.** `ctx$traits` has three correlated columns; this chapter predicted one. A multi-trait Bayesian model borrows information across traits and should out-predict fitting each one separately, especially for the traits with less training data. - **Cross-validated accuracy, not a single split.** Every accuracy number above comes from one training/candidate partition (or `genpred`'s 15 replicates of one). A real programme estimates accuracy by k-fold or forward cross-validation before trusting a model with a selection decision. - **Training-set design.** Accuracy here depends on training-set size and on how related the training records are to the candidates -- the same relatedness that makes $N_s$ (@sec-catalogue) and the founder-frequency discipline of @sec-genomic-era matter elsewhere in this book. - **Retraining across cycles.** @sec-cycles runs the *selection* side of a multi-cycle programme with a fixed, perfect index. A model trained once and never updated goes stale as the population it predicts drifts from the population it was trained on. - **Genotyping cost and marker density.** Accuracy was measured here at a fixed 2000 markers; a real programme trades marker density against genotyping cost per individual, not just against training-set size. :::
